accidents.name: Apollo 1 (Apollo 204) cabin fire
accidents.category: Electrical arc ignition of combustibles in oxygen-rich cabin
accidents.outcome: Fire and cabin rupture; crew did not escape
accidents.time: Momentary power failure 23:30:55 GMT; spacecraft rupture about 6:31:19 pm EST
accidents.initiating: Most probable initiator: electrical arc near the floor of the lower forward left-hand equipment bay, where ECS instrumentation power wiring enters the area between the Environmental Control Unit and the oxygen panel. No single ignition source conclusively identified; no evidence of sabotage.
accidents.how: Fire spread through combustible nonmetallic materials in a 100% oxygen cabin. Cabin pressure rose until the module ruptured; the inner hatch could not be opened against the internal pressure. Consciousness was lost 15-30 s after the first suit failure; resuscitation chances were lost within four minutes. Cause of death: asphyxia from toxic gases, thermal burns contributory.
accidents.damaged: Command Module cabin; lower forward left equipment bay (origin zone); crew suits (outer layers most damaged); inner hatch (could not open)
accidents.root: Pure-oxygen atmosphere at above-ambient pressure with many combustible materials near possible ignition sources; the Board called the test conditions 'extremely hazardous'.
accidents.factors: Combustibles listed in the medical analysis include nylon, polyurethane foam, neoprene, silicones and acrylics; suits could not protect the crew at this fire intensity; oxygen purge contributed to fire propagation; slow crew egress.
accidents.actions: Board recommended severely restricting and controlling combustible materials and reducing/simplifying the operations needed for crew egress.
accidents.unverified: fatalities count (3) not stated in the fetched pages; corrective actions limited to what the Board's findings page recommends

accidents.name: Apollo 13 service module oxygen tank explosion
accidents.site: In flight, about 205,000 miles from Earth
accidents.category: Cryogenic oxygen tank combustion/explosion from electrical fault
accidents.outcome: Lunar landing abandoned; crew survived using the Lunar Module as a lifeboat, splashdown 17 Apr 1970
accidents.time: About 55 h 55 min into the flight
accidents.initiating: Less than two minutes before the explosion the crew switched on the tank fans at Mission Control's request; a short circuit likely produced a spark and combustion in the damaged oxygen tank.
accidents.how: During a March 1970 ground procedure the tank heaters were powered from 65 V ground equipment although their thermostat switches were rated for 28 V DC. The switches failed to open at the 80 F design point; the heater tube likely reached about 1,000 F (the gauge read only to 85 F), damaging Teflon wire insulation. The tank was nevertheless filled with liquid oxygen. In flight, the spark in the damaged tank led to combustion and an explosion that damaged the panel over bay 4 and the high-gain antenna (temporary telemetry loss); oxygen tank 1 or its plumbing then lost pressure slowly and the fuel cells lost their oxygen.
accidents.damaged: Oxygen tank 2; heater thermostat switches and Teflon-insulated wiring; Service Module bay 4 panel; high-gain antenna; oxygen tank 1 / plumbing; fuel cells (starved of oxygen)
accidents.root: Review Board (Cortright): 'an unusual combination of mistakes coupled with a somewhat deficient and unforgiving design.'
accidents.factors: Tank dropped about two inches during redesign work in October 1968 (possible fill/drain damage); a 25 March 1970 test emptied the tank only about 8%; engineers chose not to replace the tank to avoid a costly launch delay.
accidents.actions: Redesign and recertify the SM oxygen storage system; review all cryogenic oxygen systems for materials compatibility; require complete component histories. From Apollo 14: third tank in a different bay, upgraded thermostats, fans removed, wiring sheathed in stainless steel (launch slipped from Oct 1970 to Jan 1971).
accidents.body: Apollo 13 Review Board (chair Edgar Cortright), report 15 June 1970

accidents.name: Space Shuttle Challenger (STS-51-L)
accidents.vehicle: Space Shuttle Challenger; right solid rocket booster; External Tank
accidents.site: Launch Pad 39B, Kennedy Space Center, Florida
accidents.category: Solid rocket booster joint seal failure leading to structural breakup
accidents.outcome: Vehicle broke apart over the Atlantic; crew lost
accidents.time: Liftoff 11:38 a.m. EST; breakup at about 73 s
accidents.initiating: O-ring seal failure in the aft field joint of the right solid rocket booster; exceptionally cold weather contributed.
accidents.how: Hot gas escaped through the failed seal and damaged the strut connecting the booster to the External Tank. At about 72 s hydrogen streaming from the failed tank burned explosively together with leaking liquid oxygen from the intertank. At about 73 s, under severe aerodynamic loads, the vehicle broke apart.
accidents.propellant: SRB solid propellant; External Tank liquid hydrogen / liquid oxygen
accidents.damaged: Right SRB aft field joint (O-rings); SRB-to-External-Tank attach strut; External Tank (hydrogen tank, intertank); Orbiter (breakup)
accidents.root: Design flaw in the O-ring field joint (Commission: 'an accident rooted in history').
accidents.factors: NASA and Morton Thiokol did not adequately respond to the known flaw (managers reportedly aware since 1977); Thiokol engineers recommended not launching below 53 F but senior management overruled them after an offline caucus; launch decision process 'seriously flawed' with incomplete or misleading information; unrealistic schedule; Feynman appendix: management risk estimates as low as 1 in 100,000 versus engineers' roughly 1 in 100 to 1 in 200.
accidents.unverified: launch-morning temperature not given in fetched sources; corrective actions not fetched; read the Rogers Commission Report itself before citing in a paper

accidents.name: Space Shuttle Columbia (STS-107)
accidents.vehicle: Space Shuttle Columbia; External Tank left bipod ramp foam; left wing leading edge RCC panels
accidents.category: Thermal protection damage leading to re-entry heat intrusion
accidents.outcome: Vehicle lost during re-entry; crew lost
accidents.time: Foam strike during ascent; abnormal heating preceded abnormal aerodynamic events by several minutes during re-entry
accidents.initiating: Foam from the left bipod ramp of the External Tank struck the underside of the left wing leading edge near RCC panels 6-9 (or the tiles behind them) at about 775 ft/s.
accidents.how: Columbia re-entered with a pre-existing breach in the left wing leading edge. Debris analysis identified RCC panel 8-left as the point of heat intrusion; abnormal heating preceded abnormal aerodynamic events by several minutes, and telemetry showing problems reached Mission Control only after the Orbiter had suffered unrecoverable damage. The de-orbit burn and flight path were normal until just before loss of signal.
accidents.damaged: External Tank left bipod ramp foam (debris source); left wing leading edge RCC panels 6-9 impact zone; RCC panel 8-left (heat-intrusion point)
accidents.root: Foam loss from the bipod ramp (several factors combined; subsurface defects found in dissected ramps) striking an RCC system designed with almost no impact resistance.
accidents.factors: Schedule pressure from Space Station assembly; foam shedding normalized as 'in-family' and NASA requirements not followed; debris assessment team lacked clear management ownership; imagery request routed through an institutional channel; assumptions and uncertainties did not reach decision makers; safety offices depended on Shuttle Program funding; RCC oxidation weakening could not be inspected directly.
accidents.unverified: date and crew count not in the fetched page; corrective actions not fetched; exact time of strike not given

accidents.name: Antares Orb-3 launch failure
accidents.vehicle: Orbital ATK Antares 130 with Cygnus cargo spacecraft
accidents.operator: Orbital ATK (NASA Commercial Resupply Services mission)
accidents.site: Mid-Atlantic Regional Spaceport, NASA Wallops Flight Facility, Virginia
accidents.category: Engine turbopump explosion and liquid-oxygen fire
accidents.outcome: Vehicle and cargo destroyed after range-safety destruct; pad and adjacent facilities damaged
accidents.time: About 6:22 p.m. EDT; just over 15 s after liftoff
accidents.initiating: Explosion in the E15 LO2 turbopump of the AJ26 engine in the Main Engine 1 position.
accidents.how: Loss of rotor radial positioning caused rubbing in the turbopump's Hydraulic Balance Assembly (HBA) seal package, which ignited an LO2 fire. The explosion damaged the E16 engine in the Main Engine 2 position and thrust was lost. Range safety issued a destruct command shortly before impact; the vehicle hit the ground near the pad and was totally destroyed with about 2,296 kg of pressurized cargo.
accidents.damaged: AJ26 E15 LO2 turbopump (HBA seal package, turbine-end bearing); E16 engine; launch pad and adjacent buildings; Cygnus and cargo
accidents.root: Three credible technical root causes (any one or a combination): inadequate design robustness of the AJ26 LO2 HBA and turbine-end bearing; foreign object debris (titanium and silica) in E15 (no clear link established); manufacturing/workmanship defect in the E15 turbine bearing bore housing.
accidents.body: NASA Independent Review Team and Orbital ATK investigation (same proximate cause)
accidents.unverified: corrective actions not in the executive summary text retrieved

accidents.name: SpaceX CRS-7 Falcon 9 in-flight failure
accidents.category: Pressure vessel (helium COPV) support-strut failure leading to second-stage overpressure
accidents.initiating: Preliminary: a support strut holding a helium pressurization bottle (COPV) in the second-stage LOX tank broke at about 3.2 g.
accidents.how: The buoyant bottle likely struck the tank interior and was damaged, releasing helium into the LOX tank. Telemetry showed a helium pressure drop then an unexpected rise to the starting pressure. Overpressure built within about a quarter of a second, the second stage failed and the vehicle disintegrated.
accidents.propellant: Second-stage liquid oxygen tank with helium pressurant
accidents.damaged: Helium COPV support strut; helium COPV; second-stage LOX tank; Dragon spacecraft
accidents.root: Preliminary (per SpaceX): strut failure with material weakness; strut designed for 10,000 lbf versus an estimated 2,000 lbf load. Musk called it 'a really odd failure mode' and 'somewhat speculative'.
accidents.actions: Replace struts in all future tanks, test every strut before use, use a strut with a higher safety margin (as stated by SpaceX at the time).
accidents.unverified: date and site not in the fetched article; final cause (a NASA review in 2018 reportedly cited a design error, headline only) not fetched; injuries not mentioned

accidents.name: SpaceX Falcon 9 AMOS-6 pad explosion
accidents.site: Space Launch Complex 40, Cape Canaveral Air Force Station, Florida
accidents.category: Composite overwrapped pressure vessel (COPV) failure with liquid-oxygen ignition
accidents.initiating: Failure of one of the three helium COPVs inside the second-stage liquid-oxygen tank.
accidents.how: Investigators concluded oxygen likely collected between the COPV's aluminum liner and carbon overwrap, in a void or buckle in the liner, and ignited (breaking fibers or friction can ignite oxygen in the overwrap). Helium loading temperatures were cold enough to form solid oxygen, making trapping and friction ignition more likely.
accidents.propellant: Liquid oxygen with cold helium loading
accidents.damaged: Second-stage LOX tank COPVs (three, aluminum liner with carbon overwrap); second stage; AMOS-6 satellite
accidents.root: Likely mechanism: oxygen trapped between COPV liner and overwrap ignited, as above.
accidents.unverified: time of event, damage extent, injuries and corrective actions not in the fetched article

accidents.name: Ariane 5 Flight 501 maiden-flight failure
accidents.category: Software specification/design error in inertial reference system leading to loss of control
accidents.time: Loss of guidance 37 s after main-engine ignition sequence start; about 40 s after the flight sequence began at roughly 3,700 m altitude
accidents.initiating: Both inertial reference systems failed at the same time due to specification and design errors in their software.
accidents.how: The two solid-booster nozzles swiveled to their extreme positions and, slightly later, the Vulcain engine nozzle did too, making the launcher veer abruptly. The launcher broke up and its self-destruct was correctly triggered by rupture of the electrical links between the solid boosters and the core stage.
accidents.damaged: Inertial reference system (software); solid-booster nozzles; Vulcain nozzle; entire launcher
accidents.root: Specification and design errors in the inertial reference system software.
accidents.factors: The alignment function, useful only before liftoff, was not included in simulations; equipment and system tests were not sufficiently representative; the inertial reference system and the complete flight control system were not adequately analysed or tested.
accidents.actions: Fix the inertial reference system; re-examine all embedded software; improve test realism; switch off the alignment function after liftoff.
accidents.unverified: launch site, payload and casualties not on the fetched page

accidents.name: Soyuz MS-10 launch abort
accidents.vehicle: Soyuz launcher with Soyuz MS-10 crew capsule
accidents.outcome: Capsule separated and landed on a ballistic trajectory about 200 miles from the launch point; crew uninjured
accidents.initiating: Abnormal separation of one booster, linked to a deformed separation-sensor pin believed to have been damaged during assembly at Baikonur.
accidents.how: The malfunctioning booster struck the core stage near the fuel tank, causing decompression and loss of attitude control. The emergency rescue system separated the capsule, which followed a ballistic trajectory; the system performed without issues. Crew: Nick Hague and Alexey Ovchinin.
accidents.damaged: Booster separation-sensor pin; core stage near the fuel tank
accidents.unverified: time after liftoff not given; corrective actions not in fetched article

accidents.name: Nedelin catastrophe (R-16 pad explosion)
accidents.category: Hypergolic propellant ignition on the pad during servicing
accidents.fatalities: At least 74 immediately and about 50 more later from injuries
accidents.initiating: Fuel valves in the second stage opened unintentionally.
accidents.how: The hypergolic propellants mixed and burned into the first stage, causing a massive explosion at the launch pad. Victims died from the fireball and toxic gases; Marshal Mitrofan Nedelin, in charge of the R-16 program, was killed.
accidents.damaged: Second-stage fuel valves (origin); first stage; pad area and personnel
accidents.root: Per the NASA summary: personnel and visitors near the pad exceeded safe limits while technicians were repairing a fully fuelled rocket.
accidents.unverified: Soviet-era secrecy: details and casualty figures vary by source; investigating body and corrective actions not in the fetched summary

accidents.name: Starship Ship 36 test-stand explosion
accidents.site: Massey's test facility near Starbase, Texas
accidents.category: Suspected nitrogen COPV failure during propellant loading
accidents.outcome: Ship destroyed in a large fireball; damage to the test stand and Massey's facilities unclear at the time of reporting
accidents.time: Shortly after 11 p.m. CT on 18 June 2025 (0400 UTC 19 June)
accidents.initiating: Preliminary: possible failure of a composite overwrapped pressure vessel holding gaseous nitrogen in the nosecone area.
accidents.how: The ship was ripped apart in a large fireball while liquid methane and liquid oxygen were being loaded ahead of a planned static fire of its six Raptor engines. SpaceX said all personnel were safe and accounted for.
accidents.damaged: Gaseous-nitrogen COPV in the nosecone area (suspected origin); Ship 36; test stand and Massey's facilities (extent unknown)
accidents.root: Preliminary only (full data review was ongoing at the time of the article).
accidents.unverified: final root cause; a later SpaceX update attributing the event to a failed pressurized nitrogen tank appeared in search results but was not fetched

accidents.name: Soyuz T-10-1 on-pad fire and launch escape
accidents.category: Kerosene leak from turbopump failure causing a pad fire
accidents.outcome: Rocket toppled and exploded, heavily damaging the pad; crew (Vladimir Titov, Gennady Strekalov) survived via the launch escape system
accidents.initiating: A malfunctioning valve allowed pressurized nitrogen into the kerosene fuel turbopump of the Blok B booster's RD-117 engine.
accidents.how: The pump spun up without fuel and its turbine failed; kerosene leaked at the base of the rocket and ignited within a minute. The fire burned through the ground command lines, so the abort command (sent about 10 s after the fire was noticed) went by a backup radio link needing simultaneous commands from two locations. The escape rocket fired 1.2 s later (about 11 s from fire to escape) with peak 14-17 g. The vehicle burned for about 20 hours.
accidents.propellant: Kerosene and liquid oxygen (launcher fuel); kerosene leak fed the fire
accidents.damaged: Faulty nitrogen valve (origin); RD-117 kerosene turbopump; base of the rocket (leak); ground command lines; launch pad
accidents.root: Faulty valve admitting nitrogen into the fuel turbopump.
accidents.actions: Source states corrective action was taken but gives no detail.
accidents.unverified: launch site name not stated in the fetched text (Baikonur assumed from pad naming); investigating body not stated

accidents.name: Mir space station fire (Kvant-1)
accidents.category: Solid-fuel oxygen generator (SFOG / Vika) canister fire
accidents.outcome: Station structure undamaged; some Kvant-1 panels charred; flame blocked access to a Soyuz escape vehicle; no lasting harm to crew
accidents.time: Flame lasted several minutes; smoke cleared over several hours
accidents.initiating: A solid-fuel oxygen generator canister ignited while Aleksandr Lazutkin was activating it.
accidents.how: Six people were aboard (Korzun, Kaleri, Linenger, Tsibliyev, Lazutkin, Ewald). Korzun sprayed foam from a fire extinguisher while Linenger held him in place and the others passed him two more extinguishers; the flame ultimately went out on its own. Life-support systems cleared the smoke.
accidents.damaged: SFOG canister; Kvant-1 panels (charred); access to Soyuz escape vehicle (blocked)
accidents.root: After two years of study, investigators named latex glove material accidentally introduced into the canister as the most likely culprit; hydrocarbons in the canister raised the risk.
accidents.actions: Russian officials changed emergency training for crews, ground controller response and how SFOG canisters are prepared on the ground; lessons carried into ISS design and operations.

accidents.name: Intelsat 708 / Long March 3B launch failure
accidents.category: Guidance/control hardware failure leading to crash and explosion
accidents.outcome: Rocket and satellite destroyed; nearby village destroyed
accidents.fatalities: Six (official PRC reports); other accounts estimate about 100
accidents.time: About 22 s after liftoff (15 Feb 1996, about 3:00 a.m. local time per the Cox Report; 14 Feb 1996 19:01 UTC)
accidents.initiating: PRC first attributed the failure (27 Feb 1996) to the inertial measurement unit in the guidance/control system, later revising this to deterioration of gold-aluminum wiring connections in a power amplifier for the follow-up frame torque motor within that unit.
accidents.how: The rocket tipped over before clearing the launch tower, flew roughly parallel to the ground and hit a nearby hillside; the crash explosion was estimated at 20-55 tons of TNT.
accidents.damaged: Inertial measurement unit / follow-up frame torque motor power amplifier wiring (origin); launch vehicle; Intelsat 708; nearby village
accidents.root: Per the revised PRC finding: deteriorated gold-aluminum wiring connections in the power amplifier of the follow-up frame torque motor.
accidents.body: Failure Analysis Team and Failure Investigative Committee (CGWIC), reviewed by an Independent Review Committee chaired by Loral's Wah Lim
accidents.unverified: launch site name (Xichang) not in the fetched excerpt; casualty count is disputed (6 official vs about 100 estimated); the Cox Report excerpt read covers the first 100,000 characters only

flame.scope: Cabin fire in 100% oxygen at 16.7 psia (Plugs-Out Integrated Test)
flame.fuel: Combustible nonmetallic cabin materials (nylon, polyurethane foam, neoprene, silicones, acrylics per the Board medical analysis; Velcro; Teflon-insulated wiring) in 100% O2
flame.documented: AIP summary: capsule 'ignited from the inside out' in a 'fast-burning oxygen-rich atmosphere'; fire was 'intense, uncontrollable and fast'; Velcro 'caught fire explosively in the pure-oxygen environment'. Board (S01/S02): cabin pressure rose until the module ruptured. No flame temperature or visual description in the sources read.
flame.expected: Not determinable from the sources. No measurement of this fire exists in the sources read.
flame.physics: Oxygen enrichment raises flame temperature and burn rate. Analogue only (methane, 1 atm, CEA equilibrium): 2,224 K in air versus 3,050 K in pure oxygen (T07, T06). Cabin polymers were not modelled. Heat release in a closed cabin raised pressure until rupture (S01).
flame.unverified: AIP gives cabin pressure as 5 psi, which conflicts with the Board's 16.7 psia (Board value used); flame colour and temperature not documented

flame.scope: Apollo 13 service module oxygen tank 2 combustion and rupture
flame.fuel: Teflon-insulated heater/fan wiring in liquid-oxygen tank 2 (cryogenic O2)
flame.documented: Crew reported 'an electrical event accompanied by a loud bang'; minutes later they saw the spacecraft 'venting something overboard'. A short circuit produced 'a spark resulting in a combustion event'; escaping oxygen 'at high velocity' blew off the bay 4 panel. Teflon burning in LOX was photographed only in a postflight test. No in-flight flame imagery or colour is described.
flame.expected: No external flame is documented. The combustion was inside the tank; the visible effect was venting gas/debris.
flame.physics: Heater tube estimated to have reached about 1,000 F (about 811 K) after the thermostat switches failed (gauge read only to 85 F), damaging Teflon wire insulation (T13). A spark then ignited insulation in oxygen. Many materials that burn slowly in air burn vigorously in oxygen (see FP-11).
flame.unverified: Tank temperature is an investigators estimate, not a measurement; no flame colour documented

flame.scope: Challenger: (1) SRB joint leak plume, (2) hydrogen/LOX burn after External Tank breach, (3) hypergolic orbiter burn
flame.fuel: SRB: ammonium perchlorate composite (69.93% AP, 16% aluminium, 12.04% binder, 1.96% epoxy, 0.07% iron oxide); External Tank: LH2/LOX; orbiter: hypergolic fuel with nitrogen tetroxide (per Rogers Commission text)
flame.documented: Rogers log: gray smoke puff at 0.678 s, then 'increasingly blacker smoke' to 2.5 s; first 'very small flame' on enhanced film at 58.788 s; 'continuous, well-defined plume' at 59.262 s; at 64.660 s an 'abrupt change in the plume's shape and color' (first visual sign of External Tank breach) and ~45 ms later a 'bright sustained glow'; at 73.124 s hydrogen burning 'massive, almost explosive'; 'The reddish brown colors of the hypergolic fuel burn are visible on the edge of the main fireball'; at ~76 s a 'reddish-brown cloud envelops the disintegrating Orbiter' (attributed to nitrogen tetroxide). See Flame_Timeline.
flame.colour: Gray then black smoke (0.7-2.7 s); reddish-brown (hypergolic N2O4 burn, about 73-76 s). Plume colour change at 64.66 s is stated but its colour is not given.
flame.expected: SRB plume: bright yellow-orange to white (incandescent Al/Al2O3 particles plus AlO band emission). LH2/LOX burn: faint, pale, with red-orange tint from water vapour and any sodium impurity. Inference only.
flame.physics: SRB: in open-air burns of an aluminised AP propellant the plume measured 2,300-3,000 K (T11, T12) with AlO emission at 420-550 nm; a graybody at that temperature peaks at 966-1,260 nm (computed in Flame_Temperatures), so the visible light is its short-wavelength tail (yellow-white-orange). Black smoke = burning grease, joint insulation and O-rings (Rogers). LH2/LOX: OH* emission is ultraviolet; water-vapour emission glows red/orange (S22); theoretical LOX/LH2 chamber temperature 3,610 K at 20 MPa (T02). Hypergolic red-brown: NO2 from N2O4 dissociation (FP-09).
flame.unverified: Colour of the 64.66 s plume change not stated; SRB temperatures come from an open-air test of Atlas V propellant, not Shuttle SRB measurements; no Challenger-specific flame temperature in sources read

flame.scope: Columbia re-entry: hot-gas intrusion and air-plasma glow (not a chemical flame)
flame.fuel: Not applicable: air dissociated and ionised by the bow and wing shocks during hypersonic entry
flame.documented: Observers saw a 'glowing plasma trail' (about 08:53:28 EST) and some a 'bright flash' about 08:53; video shows debris disappearing 'within her plasma trail'. Telemetry: hot gas reached the left wing leading edge within 16 s of entering maximum heating (08:50:53); sensors behind panels 9 and 10 spiked at 08:51:09; loss of signal at about Mach 18 and 201,000 ft. See Flame_Timeline.
flame.colour: Not stated in sources read (described only as 'glowing' and 'bright flash')
flame.expected: Not determinable from the sources (no chromaticity data read).
flame.physics: Shock-layer air dissociates and ionises; emitters are atomic O (777, 845 nm) and N (745, 1013, 1250 nm) lines plus ions (FP-10). Hayabusa analogue: about 10,000 K behind the shock, 5,500 K in the wake, 3,380 K heat-shield surface (T16-T18); a different vehicle, so analogue only. Secondary press gives RCC panel temperatures of about 3,000 C normally and above 8,000 C in the failure (T14, T15).
flame.unverified: The 8,000 C figure is from a press article and unclear whether it is a surface or gas temperature; plasma colour not documented; Hayabusa values are not Columbia values

flame.scope: Antares Orb-3: LO2 turbopump fire/explosion in AJ26 engine about 15 s after liftoff, then fall-back and range-safety destruct
flame.fuel: Liquid oxygen / liquid kerosene (RP-1) vehicle class (S07); failure initiated on the LO2 side
flame.documented: IRT: 'Just over 15 seconds into flight ... an explosion in the Antares Main Engine System'; 'frictional rubbing led to ignition and fire involving LO2 within the turbopump HBA'; engines lost thrust, vehicle fell back, range safety destruct shortly before impact. No flame colour, size or plume behaviour described.
flame.expected: Soot-laden kerosene/LOX fire: yellow-orange luminous flame. Inference only; the first ignition was inside the engine and has no recorded appearance.
flame.physics: In a modelled RP-1 plume the major radiators are CO2, H2O and soot (S26); soot gives a broadband graybody continuum (yellow-orange) that dominates where soot is present, while OH* (UV), CH* (about 431 nm) and C2* Swan bands (436-564 nm) are weak by comparison (S23). Theoretical LOX/RP-1 chamber temperature 3,803 K at 20 MPa, O/F 2.5 (T01); chemical rockets generally 2,500-4,100 C (T09, T10).
flame.unverified: Visible appearance of the event not documented; physics values are theoretical, not measured on this vehicle

flame.scope: SpaceX CRS-7: second-stage LOX tank overpressure 139 s after liftoff
flame.fuel: Liquid oxygen with helium pressurant (S08); Falcon 9 fuel is RP-1 (general knowledge, not stated in the page read)
flame.documented: Musk: 'There was an overpressure event in the Second Stage liquid oxygen tank'; it happened 'within a quarter of a second'; a breached helium bottle likely released helium into the LOX tank; outcome: loss of Dragon and breakup of the rocket. No fire, vapour cloud or colour described in the page read.
flame.expected: Not determinable; if RP-1 mixed with LOX after breakup, a sooty orange fireball would be expected. Inference only.
flame.physics: Kerosene/LOX flames are soot-radiation dominated (S26). Theoretical LOX/RP-1 chamber temperature 3,803 K at 20 MPa (T01). The initial event was a pressure rupture of a cryogenic tank, not a flame.
flame.unverified: Fuel type not stated on the page read; no visual description

flame.scope: Falcon 9 AMOS-6: COPV failure and fire in second-stage LOX tank on the pad
flame.fuel: Liquid oxygen with cold helium loading; solid oxygen formed by helium loading temperature (S09); RP-1 fuel (general knowledge, not in page read)
flame.documented: Investigation: one of three COPVs inside the second-stage LOX tank failed; likely mode was oxygen accumulating between liner and overwrap in a buckle; 'breaking fibers or friction can ignite the oxygen'; helium was cold enough to create solid oxygen. No description of fire, fireball or colour in the page read.
flame.expected: Not determinable; a kerosene/LOX pad fire would be expected to be sooty orange. Inference only.
flame.physics: Ignition by friction or fibre breakage of oxygen-soaked composite is a combustion-in-oxygen mechanism (FP-11). Fuel-side flame physics as ACC-05 (T01).
flame.unverified: No visual or temperature data in page read

flame.scope: Ariane 5 Flight 501: breakup and self-destruction about 40 s after ignition sequence start
flame.fuel: Two solid boosters and a Vulcain main engine (named in S10); propellant types not stated in the page read
flame.documented: ESA: vehicle 'veered off its flight path, broke up and exploded' at about 3,700 m; self-destruction 'correctly triggered by rupture of the electrical links' between boosters and core stage. No flame description.
flame.physics: If the boosters are aluminised ammonium-perchlorate composite and the core is LH2/LOX (general knowledge, not in the page read), the physics of ACC-03 applies: particle-laden bright plume (T11, T12) plus faint hydrogen flame (FP-05).
flame.unverified: Propellant types and visual appearance not documented in the page read

flame.fuel: Not documented in this dataset (propellant_or_atmosphere = None)
flame.documented: No flame or fire observation is recorded in this dataset or the sources read for this pass.
flame.physics: No flame physics assigned; no combustion event documented.
flame.unverified: S11 was not re-read in this pass; row left empty rather than inferred

flame.fuel: Hypergolic propellants (S12). Oxidiser identity not stated in the page read.
flame.documented: NASA SMA: second-stage fuel valves 'inadvertently opened'; hypergolic propellants 'mixed and burned into the first stage'; 'massive explosion at the launch pad'; 'at least 74 people died from the fireball and toxic gases'. Colour and temperature not described.
flame.expected: If the oxidiser was nitrogen tetroxide or red fuming nitric acid, a reddish-brown/orange cloud would be expected; the oxidiser is not confirmed in the sources read.
flame.physics: Hypergolic propellants ignite on contact without an ignition source. N2O4 dissociates to NO2, which is reddish-brown; red fuming nitric acid gives similar red clouds (S31, FP-09). No temperature obtained for N2O4/UDMH.
flame.unverified: Oxidiser identity (R-16 is commonly reported to use a nitric-acid/N2O4 oxidiser with UDMH) not confirmed in sources read; no colour or temperature data

flame.fuel: Liquid methane and liquid oxygen being loaded; GN2 COPV in nosecone failed (preliminary)
flame.documented: Spaceflight Now: vehicle 'ripped apart in a giant fireball' while methane and LOX were being loaded, shortly after 11 p.m. CT (0400 UTC) 18/19 June 2025; SpaceX preliminary analysis pointed to a COPV holding gaseous nitrogen in the nosecone. No colour described.
flame.expected: Not determinable. Methane/oxygen flames show weaker soot luminosity than kerosene in laboratory flames; a large open-air fireball can still be luminous. Inference only.
flame.physics: LOX/methane flame emission: OH* about 307 nm (UV), CH* about 431-436 nm (blue), C2* Swan bands 436-564 nm; above 60 bar a visible continuum around 450-700 nm becomes the strongest visible feature in engine chambers (S24), which does not apply to an open-air fireball at about 1 atm. No blackbody radiation was seen in low-pressure laboratory methane/O2 flames (S23). Theoretical LOX/CH4 chamber temperature 3,589 K at 20 MPa, O/F 3.0 (T04).
flame.unverified: Cause is preliminary; fireball colour and temperature not documented; lab flame data do not transfer directly to a fireball

flame.fuel: Kerosene (S14) with liquid oxygen (dataset); kerosene leaked from a failed fuel turbopump at the base
flame.documented: Valve fault let pressurised nitrogen into the kerosene turbopump about 90 s before launch; 'within a minute' spilled kerosene ignited; fire had burned through ground command lines before it was noticed; abort command ~10 s after the fire was noticed, escape system fired 1.2 s later 'as flames engulfed the Soyuz launch vehicle'; 3-4 s later the vehicle 'toppled over and exploded'; remains burned for another 20 hours. Colour and temperature not described. See Flame_Timeline.
flame.expected: Sooty orange-yellow kerosene pool fire. Inference only.
flame.physics: Liquid kerosene burns with a luminous soot flame (soot is a major radiator in kerosene combustion, S26). Theoretical LOX/RP-1 chamber temperature (T01) is for engine conditions, not an open pool fire.
flame.unverified: No visual or temperature description in S14; pool-fire temperature not obtained

flame.scope: Mir Kvant-1 fire from a solid-fuel oxygen generator canister
flame.fuel: Solid-fuel oxygen generator (Vika/TGK) burning canisters of lithium perchlorate per NASA; supplies oxygen for one crew member per day
flame.documented: NASA: the canister shot 'a three-foot flame with sparks and bits of molten metal across the module'; flame 'lasting several minutes' blocked the evacuation route to the Soyuz; 'dense smoke' filled the modules and was cleared over several hours; the flame 'finally extinguished itself'. Colour and temperature not stated.
flame.expected: Not determinable. Molten-metal sparks imply incandescent particles (bright orange-white); inference only.
flame.physics: A chemical oxygen candle decomposes a perchlorate to release oxygen and burns its fuel in that oxygen; it is oxygen-rich and cannot be smothered by removing air. Sparks and molten metal indicate hot incandescent metal particles. No temperature in the source (the generator burn temperature was not obtained).
flame.unverified: Oxidiser chemistry as stated by NASA article (lithium perchlorate); other sources name different salts, so check; no colour or temperature

flame.scope: Intelsat 708 / Long March 3B: crash 22 s after liftoff
flame.fuel: Long March 3B uses N2O4/UDMH (S31); stage and booster details not read in S16
flame.documented: Cox Report: rocket 'tipped over', 'crashed into a nearby hillside' about 22 s after liftoff; 'the crash created an explosion that was roughly equivalent to 20 to 55 tons of TNT. It destroyed a nearby village.' Fire and colour not described in the part read.

flame.expected: Reddish-brown/orange NO2-bearing cloud with orange flame. Inference from the propellant.
flame.physics: N2O4/UDMH exhaust is described as 'rusty red', 'bright orange-red'; the colour comes from NO2 formed when N2O4 breaks down in heat (S31, FP-09). No temperature obtained for N2O4/UDMH (T03 is LOX/UDMH and is not applicable).
flame.unverified: Only the first 100,000 characters of S16 were read; the Cox Report gives 15 Feb 1996 about 03:00 local time while Accidents lists 1996-02-14 (likely UTC)

mechanisms.name: Soot incandescence (blackbody)
mechanisms.spectrum: Continuous spectrum peaking in the infrared
mechanisms.why: Fuel-rich zones make soot that is heated to incandescence. Emission follows Planck blackbody radiation; the visible part is the short-wavelength tail, so cooler soot looks orange and hotter soot looks yellow-white. A flame colour gives only a rough temperature estimate.
mechanisms.numbers: Peak wavelength = Wien constant / T (Flame_Data column O). Bunsen yellow flame peak about 2,000 K (F16).

mechanisms.name: Radical chemiluminescence (CH, C2)
mechanisms.spectrum: Band emission, Swan bands in the blue and green; mostly below about 565 nm
mechanisms.why: Excited CH and C2 radicals emit light directly. This blue shows when soot is scarce, such as in a clean premixed flame; soot light masks it otherwise.
mechanisms.numbers: Visible output of sootless hydrocarbon flames lies largely below about 565 nm (F16).

mechanisms.name: Hydrogen flame emission
mechanisms.colour: Nearly invisible in daylight; faint pale blue
mechanisms.spectrum: UV band from OH* near 305-325 nm; infrared water-vapour bands
mechanisms.why: Hydrogen burns to water with no soot, so almost no visible light is emitted. Most emission is ultraviolet and infrared, which is why hydrogen flames need UV or IR detectors.
mechanisms.numbers: OH* peak about 309-310 nm; hydrogen flames radiate little IR heat but substantial UV.

mechanisms.name: Sodium and potassium impurities
mechanisms.why: Trace sodium (from sodium hydride in the hydrogen supply) is excited in the flame and tints it orange. NASA measured sodium in the SSME exit plane and treated it as the main visible tint of hydrogen-oxygen exhaust.
mechanisms.numbers: Time-average sodium 0.091 parts per billion at the SSME exit plane (F09). Sodium D wavelength is a standard value not retrieved here.

mechanisms.name: Water-vapour emission in hydrogen flames
mechanisms.why: Hot water vapour emits an orange-red to infrared continuum. At high altitude and low density the plume looks nearly clear; at atmospheric pressure the denser products show the colour.
mechanisms.numbers: LH2/LOX plume described by NASA engineers as nearly clear but not entirely clear (F09).

mechanisms.name: Nitrogen dioxide from N2O4 oxidiser
mechanisms.why: Nitrogen tetroxide is in equilibrium with brown NO2, so nitrogen-oxide-bearing burns and clouds look reddish-brown. The Rogers Commission documented a reddish-brown hypergolic burn in the Challenger breakup.
mechanisms.numbers: Observation documented (F01). The NO2 explanation is an inference not stated in that passage.

mechanisms.name: Burning metal and incandescent oxide
mechanisms.colour: White to orange sparks and globules
mechanisms.why: Metals ignited in an oxygen-rich jet burn white-hot and shed molten globules. Apollo 13 tests showed aluminium components could ignite; Mir crew saw molten metal splattering. Solid-motor alumina glow is expected but no source was retrieved.
mechanisms.numbers: Mir flame about 3 ft (0.9 m) with sparks and molten metal (F13).

mechanisms.name: Re-entry shock-layer air plasma
mechanisms.spectrum: Atomic and molecular air emission (not retrieved)
mechanisms.why: Hypersonic heating dissociates and ionises air in the shock layer. Surface temperatures on the wing leading edge normally reach about 2,650-3,000 F. Investigators found RCC eroded to knife edges near the breach.
mechanisms.numbers: Normal leading-edge temperature 2,650 F at EI+471 s, 3,000 F at EI+651 s (F07).

mechanisms.name: Oxygen-enriched combustion
mechanisms.why: Raising oxygen concentration and pressure makes ordinary materials ignite more easily and spread fire faster. The Apollo 204 Board found the 100% oxygen purge contributed to fire propagation and that early flames were relatively smokeless.
mechanisms.numbers: 16.7 psia, 100% O2 in Apollo 1; peak cabin pressure at least 29 psia at rupture (F03).

mechanisms.name: Gravity effect on flame spread
mechanisms.why: Without buoyant convection a flame along a wire spreads more slowly and less vigorously. Apollo 13 zero-g tests found about half the 1 g spread rate for Teflon wire in dense oxygen.
mechanisms.numbers: 0.12-0.32 in/s in zero-g versus 0.55 in/s at 1 g (F05).
